{{short description|Equivalence of notions of density for sets of multiples of integers}}
{{Use dmy dates|cs1-dates=ly|date=February 2025}}
{{Use list-defined references|date=February 2025}}
{{CS1 config|mode=cs2}}
In [[number theory]], the '''Davenport–Erdős theorem''' states that, for sets of multiples of integers, several different notions of [[Natural density|density]] are equivalent.{{r|ak|h|t}}

Let <math>A=a_1,a_2,\dots</math> be a sequence of [[positive integer]]s. Then the multiples of <math>A</math> are another set <math>M(A)</math> that can be defined as the set <math>M(A)=\{ka\mid k\in\mathbb{N}, a\in A\}</math> of numbers formed by multiplying members of <math>A</math> by arbitrary positive integers.{{r|ak|h|t}}

According to the Davenport–Erdős theorem, for a set <math>M(A)</math>, the following notions of density are equivalent, in the sense that they all produce the same number as each other for the density of <math>M(A)</math>:{{r|ak|h|t}}
*The lower [[natural density]], the [[Limit superior and limit inferior|inferior limit]] as <math>n</math> goes to infinity of the proportion of members of <math>M(A)</math> in the interval <math>[1,n]</math>.
*The [[logarithmic density]] or multiplicative density, the weighted proportion of members of <math>M(A)</math> in the interval <math>[1,n]</math>, again in the limit, where the weight of an element <math>a</math> is <math>1/a</math>.
*The sequential density, defined as the limit (as <math>i</math> goes to infinity) of the densities of the sets <math>M(\{a_1,\dots a_i\})</math> of multiples of the first <math>i</math> elements of <math>A</math>. As these sets can be decomposed into finitely many disjoint [[arithmetic progression]]s, their densities are well defined without resort to limits.

A [[Behrend sequence]] is defined as a sequence <math>A</math> for which the three densities <math>M(A)</math> described by this theorem equal one.{{r|ht}} In this case, the  upper natural density (taken using the [[Limit superior and limit inferior|superior limit]] in place of the inferior limit) and the natural density itself (the limit of the same sequence of values) must also equal one. However, there exist other sequences <math>A</math> and their sets of multiples <math>M(A)</math> for which the upper natural density differs from the lower density, and for which the natural density itself does not exist.{{r|b}}

The theorem is named after [[Harold Davenport]] and [[Paul Erdős]], who published it in 1936.{{r|de1}} Their original proof used the [[Hardy–Littlewood Tauberian theorem]]; later, they published another, elementary proof.{{r|de2}}
